la:verb:committo.html:
com-mitto (con-m-), mīsi, missum, 3, v. a.
Of two or more objects, to bring, join, combine into one whole; to join or put together, to connect, unite.
In gen. (rare; not in Cic.), constr. inter se, cum aliquā re, alicui, with in and acc., and with acc. only.
Inter se: res in ordinem digestae atque inter se commissae,: per nondum commissa inter se munimenta urbem intravit,; cf. thus with inter se: oras vulneris suturis,: duo verba,: easdem litteras,: duo comparativa,.—
With cum: costae committuntur cum osse pectoris,.—
With dat.: viam a Placentiā ut Flaminiae committeret,: quā naris fronti committitur,is joined to,: quā vir equo commissus erat, (of a Centaur); cf. of Scylla: delphinum caudas utero commissa luporum,: commissa dextera dextrae,: medulla spinae commissa cerebro,: moles, quae urbem continenti committeret,; Duker.—
With in and acc.: commissa in unum crura,: committuntur suturae in unguem,.—(ε) With acc. only: barbaricam pestem navibus obtulit, commissam infabre, Pac. ap. (Trag. Rel. v. 271 Rib.): commissis operibus,: fidibusque mei commissa mariti moenia,: (terra) maria committeret,; : noctes duas,; cf.: nocte commissā. : commissa corpore toto,; Lucil. ap. : cervix committitur primo

artu, : domus plumbo commissa,patched,.—

In partic., to set or bring men or animals together in a contest or fight, as competitors, etc., to set together, set on (freq. in Suet.; elsewhere rare): pugiles Latinos cum Graecis,: quingenis peditibus, elephantis vicenis, tricenis equitibus hinc et inde commissis,; : camelorum quadrigas,; : victores committe,; cf. : licet Aenean Rutulumque ferocem Committas,i.e. you describe their contest in your poem, you bring them in contact with each other,: eunucho Bromium committere noli,: inter se omnes,: aequales inter se,.—
Trop., to bring together for comparison, to compare, put together, match: committit vates et comparat, inde Maronem, Atque aliā parte in trutinā suspendit Homerum,; cf. ; .—
Transf., of a battle, war: proelium, certamen, bellum, etc.
To arrange a battle or contest, to enter upon, engage in, begin, join, commence, : proelii committendi signum dare,: cum proelium commissum audissent,: commisso ab equitibus proelio,: in aciem exercitum eduxit proeliumque commisit,; ; ; ; ; : postquam eo ventum est, ut a ferentariis proelium committi posset,: commisso proelio, diutius nostrorum militum impetum hostes ferre non potuerunt,; ; Kraner ad loc.: Caesar cohortatus suos proelium commisit,: utrum proelium committi ex usu esset, necne,; 1, 52; 2, 19; : pridie quam Siciliensem pugnam classe committeret,: avidus committere pugnam,: pugnas,: rixae committendae causā,: cum vates monere eum (regem) coepit, ne committeret, aut certe differret obsidionem,.—Of a drinking contest for a wager: a summo septenis cyathis committe hos ludos,: nondum commisso spectaculo,: musicum agona,: aciem,: commissum (bellum) ac profligatum conficere,; ; ; cf.: si quis trium temporum momenta consideret, primo commissum bellum, profligatum secundo, tertio vero confectum est,: committere Martem,: quo die ludi committebantur,: ludos dedicationis,: ludos,.—
In gen., to maintain a contest, etc., to fight a battle, to hold, celebrate games, etc. (rare): illam pugnam navalem... mediocri certamine commissam arbitraris?: levia inde proelia per quatriduum commissa,: commisso modico certamine,.—
Absol. (post-Aug. and rare): contra quem Sulla iterum commisit,; ; : priusquam committeretur,before the contest began,.—
In gen.: committere aliquid, to begin any course of action, to undertake, carry on, hold (rare): tribuni sanguine commissa proscriptio,: judicium inter sicarios committitur,. —In part. perf.: egregie ad ultimum in audacter commisso perseveravit,; cf. § 8; 44, 6, 14.—
In partic., to practise or perpetrate wrong, do injustice; to commit a crime (very freq. and class.).
With acc.: ut neque timeant, qui nihil commiserint, et poenam semper ante oculos versari putent, qui peccaverint,; cf. : commississe cavet quod mox mutare laboret,: ego etiam quae tu sine Verre commisisti, Verri crimini daturus sum,: quantum flagitii,: tantum facinus,: virilis audaciae facinora,: majus delictum,: nil nefandum,: nefarias res,: scelus,; : adulterium,; : incestum cum filio,: parricidium,: caedem,; ; : sacrilegium,: fraudem,, 28, 31.—Aliquid adversus, in, erga: committere multa et in deos et in homines impie nefarieque,; cf.: in te,: aliquid adversus populum Romanum,: aliquid erga te,.—
Committere contra legem, in legem, lege, to offend, sin, commit an offence: quasi committeret contra legem,: in legem Juliam de adulteriis,; : adversus testamentum,: ne lege censoriā committant,: lege de sicariis,. —
Absol.: hoc si in posterum edixisses, minus esset nefarium... nemo enim committeret,.—
With ut, to be guilty or be in fault, so that, to give occasion or cause, that, to act so as that: id me commissurum ut patiar fieri,: non committet hodie iterum ut vapulet,: ego nolo quemquam civem committere, ut morte multandus sit: tu, etiam si commiserit, conservandum putas,: committere ut accusator nominere,; so : non committam, ut tibi ipse insanire videar,; ; ; ; ; ; Brut. ap. , ; ; .—More rare in a like sense, (ε) With cur or quare: Caedicius negare se commissurum, cur sibi quisquam imperium finiret,: neque commissum a se, quare timeret,.—(ζ) With inf.: non committunt scamna facere,: infelix committit saepe repelli,.—
Poenam, multam, etc., jurid. t. t., to bring punishment upon one's self by an error or fault, to incur, make one's self liable to it: poenam,; cf. ; and: committere in poenam edicti,: ut illam multam non commiserit,; pr.—
Committi, with a definite object, to be forfeited or confiscated, as a penalty: hereditas Veneri Erycinae commissa,; ; so, commissae hypothecae,: commissa tibi fiducia,: merces,: mancipium,: praedia in publicum,: hanc devotionem capitis esse commissam,incurred,.—
Also (mostly in jurid. Lat.) of laws, judicial regulations, promises, etc., that become binding in consequence of the fulfilment of a condition as the commission of a crime, etc.: in civitatem obligatam sponsione commissa iratis omnibus diis,a promise the condition of which has been fulfilled, Weissenb. ad loc.; cf.: hanc ego devotionem capitis mei... convictam esse et commissam putabo,: si alius committat edictum,transgresses, incurs its penalty, makes himself liable to,; cf.: commisso edicto ab alio filio, ib. lex 8, § 4: commisso per alium edicto, ib. lex 10, § 1 al.: statim atque commissa lex est,: committetur stipulatio,.
To place a thing somewhere for preservation, protection, care, etc.; to give, intrust, commit to, to give up or resign to, to trust (syn.: commendo, trado, credo; very freq. and class.); constr. with aliquid (aliquem) alicui, in aliquid, or absol.
Aliquid (aliquem, se) alicui: honor non solum datus sed etiam creditus ac commissus,: nec illi (Catoni) committendum illud negotium, sed inponendum putaverunt,: qui capita vestra non dubitatis credere, cui calceandos nemo commisit pedes?: ego me tuae commendo et committo fidei, (cf. ): ne quid committam tibi,; ; ; cf.: his salutem nostram, his fortunas, his liberos rectissime committi arbitramur,; ; cf. § 4: tibi rem magnam,; : quia commissi sunt eis magistratus,: summum imperium potestatemque omnium rerum alicui,: domino rem omnem,: caput tonsori,: ratem pelago,: sulcis semina (corresp. with spem credere terrae),; cf.: committere semen sitienti solo,, 8, 4: ulcus frigori,, n. 2: aliquid litteris,; so, verba tabellis,: vivunt commissi calores Aeoliae fidibus puellae,: committere se populo, senatui, publicis praesidiis et armis (corresp. with se tradere),; so, se urbi,: se theatro populoque Romano,: se proelio,: se pugnae,: se publico,to venture into the streets,: se neque navigationi, neque viae,; cf. ; : se timidius fortunae,: civilibus fluctibus,—Prov.: ovem lupo (Gr. καταλείπειν ὄϊν ἐν λύκοισι), .—
Aliquid (aliquem, se) in aliquid (so esp. freq. in Liv.): aliquid in alicujus fidem committere,; cf. : se in id conclave,: se in conspectum populi Romani,; cf. Pompei. ap. , C, 2: se in senatum,; : summae fuisse dementiae dubiā spe impulsum certum in periculum se committere,: rem in casum ancipitis eventus,; cf.: duos filios in aleam ejus casus,: rem in aciem,; cf.: se in aciem,; ; rempublicam in discrimen,; cf.: rerum summam in discrimen,. —
Simply alicui, or entirely absol.: sanan' es, Quae isti committas?in trusting to him,: ei commisi et credidi, Ter, Heaut. 5, 2, 13: haec cum scirem et cogitarem, commisi tamen, judices, Heio,: universo populo neque ipse committit neque illi horum consiliorum auctores committi recte putant posse,: venti, quibus necessario committendum existimabat,: sed quoniam non es veritus concredere nobis, accipe commissae munera laetitiae,intrusted,: instant enim (adversarii) et saepe discrimen omne committunt, quod deesse nobis putant,often hazard the most important advantage,: cum senatus ei commiserit, ut videret, ne quid res publica detrimenti caperet,.—With de: iste negat se de existimatione suā cuiquam nisi suis commissurum,. —Hence, P. a. as subst.: commissum, i, n.
(Acc. to I. 3.) An undertaking, enterprise: nec aliud restabat quam audacter commissum corrigere,: supererat nihil aliud in temere commisso, quam, etc.,.—
(Acc. to I. 4.) A transgression, offence, fault, crime: sacrum,: nisi aut quid commissi aut est causa jurgi,: ecquod hujus factum aut commissum non dicam audacius, sed quod, etc.,; cf. turpe,: commissi praemia,.—In plur.: post mihi non simili poenā commissa luetis,offences,; so, fateri,: improba,.—
Jurid. Lat., an incurring of fines, a confiscation or confiscated property, : in commissum cadere,: causa commissi,; fin.: aliquid pro commisso tenetur,.—
(Acc. to II.) That which is intrusted, a secret, trust: enuntiare commissa,: commissa celare,; cf. : commissa tacere,: prodere,: retinent commissa fideliter aures,: commissum teges (corresp. with arcanum scrutaberis),; cf. .

la:verb:commemoro.html:
com-mĕmŏro (conm-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to recall an object to memory in all its particulars.
Rarely of one's self, to call to mind, be mindful of, keep in mind, remember; with acc. and inf. or rel. -clause: quid quoque die dixerim, audierim, egerim, commemoro vesperi,.—With acc. and inf.: cottidie commemorabam te unum in tanto exercitu mihi fuisse adsensorem,: vitandi rumoris causā, quo patrem Caesarem vulgo reprehensum commemorabam,.—More freq.,
Of others, to bring something to one's recollection by speaking of it, to remind of: aliquid,; : ad commemorandam renovandamque amicitiam missi,: beneficia meminisse debet is, in quem collata sunt, non commemorare qui contulit,.—Hence (and so most freq.),
Without the access. idea of remembering, to make mention of something, to recount, relate; constr. with acc., acc. and inf., rel.clause, or with de.
With acc.: id interdum furtim nomen commemorabitur,: res,: causas,: humanam societatem,: Xenophontis illam jucunditatem,: o commemoranda judicia!; cf. .—
With acc. and inf., ; cf. .—
With rel.clause: quid ego nunc commemorem Singillatim, qualis ego in hunc fuerim?; : chlamydem hanc commemores quanti conducta'st?.—
With de: omnes de tuā virtute commemorant,; so ; ; ; cf.: multa de aliqua re,; .—(ε) With in: quae si in privatis gloriosa sunt, multo magis commemorabuntur in regibus,; cf.: cum legent in ejus virtutibus commemorari saltasse eum commode, Nep. praef. § 1.

la:adj:commodus.html:
com-mŏdus, a, um, adj.,
that has a due or proper measure; hence,
Object., complete, perfect, of full weight or measure, fit, suitable, due, proper, etc. (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose; most freq. in Plaut.): statura,a tall stature,: capillus,: viginti argenti minae,full twenty, (cf. : minae bonae); : talentum argenti,; Lucil. ap. : novem cyathis commodis miscentur pocula,: alimenta,: capitis valetudo commodior,more firm,; ; and transf. to the person: vivere filium atque etiam commodiorem esse,to be better,.—
Subject., suitable, fit, convenient, opportune, commodious, easy, appropriate for some one or something, favorable, friendly to (in every period and species of composition); constr. with dat. or absol., rarely with ad (v. the foll.).
Of things.
With dat.
Of the purpose or use: curationi omnia commodiora,: nec pecori opportuna seges nec commoda Baccho,.—
Of the person: hoc et vobis et meae commodum famae arbitror,: quod erit mihi bonum et commodum,: nulla lex satis commoda omnibus est (corresp. with prodesse),: primordia eloquentiae mortalibus,: hanc sibi commodissimam belli rationem judicavit,: quae sit stella homini commoda, quaeque mala,—
Absol.: hiberna,: longius ceterum commodius iter,; cf.: commodissimus in Britanniam transjectus,: commodius anni tempus,; cf. : faciliore ac commodiore judicio,: litterae satis commodae de Britannicis rebus,: mores,: commodissimum esse statuit, omnes naves subduci, etc.,.—
With or without dat. pers. in the phrase commodum est, it pleases, is agreeable, = libet: proinde ut commodum est,; : dum erit commodum, : si id non commodum est,; ; Ascon.; 2, 2, 16, § 39; 2, 1, 26, § 65; 2, 3, 70, § 165; ; ; : id si tibi erit commodum, cures velim,; ; .—
With ad and acc. of purpose (very rare): nec satis ad cursus commoda vestis Erat,.—
With sup. in u (rare): hoc exornationis genus ... commodum est auditu,.—
Of persons, serving a neighbor or (more freq.) accommodating one's self to his wishes, useful, serviceable, pleasant, agreeable, obliging, neighborly, friendly, polite, affable, gentle, etc.: mihi commodus uni,; cf. : quemquamne existimas Catone commodiorem, communiorem, moderatiorem fuisse ad omnem rationem humanitatis?: commodior mitiorque,: Apronius, qui aliis inhumanus ac barbarus, isti uni commodus ac disertus,: convivae,; cf.: commodus comissator,; and: commodus meis sodalibus,: homines,: mulier commoda, Faceta,; cf. .—In a double sense with I. supra: ubi tu commoda's, capillum commodum esse credito,.—Poet., of the measure of iambic verse: spondeos in jura paterna recepit Commodus et patiens,sharing the paternal rights with them, in a fraternal manner,.—Hence,
Subst.: commŏdum, i, n.
A convenient opportunity, favorable condition, convenience (rare, but in good prose): nostrum exspectare,: cum tamdiu sedens meum commodum exspectet,; 12, 38, 1: velim aliquando, cum erit tuum commodum, Lentulum puerum visas,when it shall be convenient for you,.—More freq.,
In the connection commodo meo, tuo, etc., per commodum, ex commodo, at, or according to my, thy, etc., convenience, conveniently, at one's leisure: etiamsi spatium ad dicendum nostro commodo vacuosque dies habuissemus,according to our convenience,: quod commodo tuo fiat,; ; : suo commodo me convenire, Caes. ap. : ubi consul copias per commodum exponere posset,: tamquam lecturus ex commodo,; ; so opp. festinanter,.—
Advantage, profit (very freq. in all periods and species of composition): commodum est, quod plus usus habet quam molestiae: bonum sincerum debet esse et ab omni parte innoxium,: ut malis gaudeant atque ex incommodis Alterius sua ut comparent commoda,: ut ex illius commodo meum compararem commodum,; cf. ; : cui tam subito tot congruerint commoda,: (honestatem) ipsam suo splendore ad se animos ducere, nullo prorsus commodo extrinsecus posito, Fragm. ap. Aug. contr. Ac. 3, 7, 15 (IV. 2, p. 470 Orell.): sequi matris commodum,: pacis,: contra valetudinis commodum laborare,to the injury of health,: mea,: in publica peccem,; cf.: populi commoda,.—
Specif., a reward, pay, stipend, salary, wages for public service: veteranorum, Brut. et Cass. ap. : omnibus provincialibus ornamentis commodisque depositis,emoluments,; ; cf.: emeritae militiae,; ; cf. also ; : militibus commoda dare,: tribunatus,: missionum,.—
A favor, privilege, immunity, ; .—
A useful thing, a good: commoda vitae,; ; cf.: cetera opinione bona sunt... proprietas in illis boni non est. Itaque commoda vocentur,: inter commoda illas (divitias) numeratis: atqui eādem ratione ne commodum quidem erunt,. —
Sometimes commodo or per commodum, adverb. antith. to that which is

injurious, without injury or detriment: ut regem reducas, quod commodo rei publicae facere possis,: si per commodum reipublicae posset, Romam venisset,.—

Concr., = commodatum, that which is lent, a loan: qui forum et basilicas commodis hospitum, non furtis nocentium ornarent,; cf. .—
Advv.:
commŏdum, adv. temp. (only in colloquial lang. and post-class. prose writers).
At a fit time, just in time, at the very nick, at the very moment, opportunely, seasonably ( = opportune, εὐκαίρως): ecce autem commodum aperitur foris,: commodum adveni domum,: orditur loqui,: ipse exit Lesbonicus,: εὐκαίρως ad me venit, cum haberem Dolabellam, Torquatus... commodum egeram diligentissime, ; . —
To designate a point of time that corresponds with another, or that just precedes it, just, just then, just now.
Absol.: ad te hercle ibam commodum,; : Taurus, sectatoribus commodum dimissis, sedebat, etc.,: si istac ibis, commodum obviam venies patri,just meet,. —
With postquam or (more freq.) with cum in a parallel clause: postquam me misisti ad portum cum luci simul, Commodum radiosus ecce sol superabat ex mari,: quom huc respicio ad virginem, Illa sese interea commodum huc advorterat,: commodum discesseras heri, cum Trebatius venit,: emerseram commodum ex Antiati in Appiam, cum in me incurrit Curio, B. and K. (al. commode); so with the pluperf. and a foll. cum, ; 13, 30, 2; 10, 16, 1; : adducitur a Veneriis Lollius commodum cum Apronius e palaestrā redisset, B. and K. (Zumpt, commode): cum jam filiae nostrae dies natalis appeteret, commodum aderant, quae muneri miseratis,. —
commŏdŏ, adv. temp., = commodum, a., just in time, seasonably, just at this time (ante-class. and very rare): commodo eccum exit, Titin. ap. P. (i. e. in tempore, Charis.): commodo de parte superiore descendebat, Sisenn. ib.: commodo dictitemus, Plaut. Fragm. ap. ; cf. p. 177.—
commŏdē, adv.
(Acc. to commodus, I.) Duly, properly, completely, rightly, well, skilfully, neatly, etc. (class.): suo quique loco viden' capillus satis compositu'st commode?: commode amictus non sum, id. Fragm. ap. : saltare, Nep. praef. § 1: legere,; cf. in comp., : multa breviter et commode dicta,; cf. ; ; ; : cogitare,: audire,: valere,: feceris commode mihique gratum, si, etc.,: commode facere, quod, etc.,; in comp.: commodius fecissent tribuni plebis, si, etc.,.—In medic.: commode facere,to do well, be beneficial,.—
(Acc. to commodus, II.)
Conveniently, suitably, opportunely, fitly, aptly, appropriately: magis commode quam strenue navigavi,: ille satis scite et commode tempus ad te cepit adeundi,: vos istic commodissime sperem esse,: explorat, quo commodissime itinere valles transiri possit,: hoc ego commodius quam tu vivo,; cf.: consumere vitiatum commodius quam integrum,; : cui commodissime subjungitur,; cf. .—
In a friendly manner, pleasantly, gently, kindly: acceptae bene et commode eximus,; ; .—
(Equiv. to commodum, adv. b.) Just, just at the moment when, etc.; only v.l. in the doubtful passages cited supra, commodum, b. fin.

la:verb:commoveo.gloss: to move something in violent motion, move; shake, stir, shift, agitate
senses: to move something in violent motion, move; shake, stir, shift, agitate
to remove something from somewhere, carry away, displace
to start, set in motion, stimulate, begin, move
to drive back, dislodge, refute, confute
to throw into disorder, unbalance, unsettle, disturb
to excite, rouse, stir up, affect, influence
la:verb:commoveo.html:
com-mŏvĕo (conm-), mōvi, mōtum, 2 (contr. forms:
commōrunt,; commōrat, Turp. ap. ; ; commōrit, Cael. ap. ; ; commossem,; commosset,; commosse,, § 96; ), v. a., to put something in violent motion, to move; both of removing from a place and backwards and forwards in a place; to shake, stir (freq. in every period and species of composition).
Lit.
To remove from a place, to carry away, displace, to start, set in motion, move: neque miser me commovere possum prae formidine,; : facilius est currentem incitare quam commovere languentem,: columnas,: castra ex eo loco,to move forward, decamp,, § 96; cf. aciem,to set the line in motion,; : se ex eo loco,: se domo,: me Thessalonicā,: te istinc,: agmen loco. to force back, cause to retreat, Sisenn. ap. ; so, hostem,; : cervum,: molem,: nummum,i. e. to use in business, (1, 1); : ais, si una littera commota sit, fore tota ut labet disciplina. Utrum igitur tibi litteram videor an totas paginas commovere?.—Sacra, t. t., to move or carry about the sacred utensils, images, etc., for religious use, Serv.; cf. : ancilia,: tripodes,.—Hence, humorously: mea si commovi sacra, if I put my instruments (artifices, tricks, etc.) in motion, . —Prov.: glaebam commosset in agro decumano Siciliae nemo,would have stirred a clod,.—
To set in motion in a place, to move hither and thither, to shake, agitate, disturb.
Of things: magni commorunt aequora venti,: alas,; cf.: penna commota volucris,; . —
Of persons, with se: quis sese commovere potest, cujus ille (sc. Roscius) vitia non videat?can stir,: num infitiari potes te... meā diligentiā circumclusum commovere te contra rem publicam non potuisse,; ; ; cf.: Lanuvii hastam se commovisse,.—
Trop.
(Acc. to I. A.) To move, drive back, distodge, refute, confute: nunc comminus agamus experiamurque, si possimus cornua commovere disputationis tuae,: si convellere adoriamur ea, quae commoveri non possunt,.—
(Acc. to I. B.) To throw into disorder, physical or mental; to unbalance, unsettle, shake, disturb (rare but class.): adflantur alii sidere, alii commoventur statis temporibus alvo, nervis, capite, mente,: perleviter commotus fuerat ... (postea) eum vidi plane integrum,: Bacchi sacris commota, Poët. ap. : commotus habebitur, i. e. mente captus,frantic, crazed,; cf.: commota mens,; ; and: commotus mente,.—
To move in mind or feeling, to make an impression upon, to excite, rouse, shake, disquiet, disturb, affect, etc.
With abl.: commorat hominem lacrimis, Turp. ap. : aliquem nimiā longinquitate locorum ac desiderio suorum,: aut libidine aliquā aut metu,; (12, 26): ludis,: quis enim, cum sibi fingit aliquid et cogitatione depingit, non simul ac se ipse commovit atque ad se revocavit, sentit, etc.,aroused,: et amore fraterno et existimatione vulgi,: adfectibus,: doctā voce,: cujus atrocitate,: vix sum apud me, ita animus commotu'st metu, Spe, gaudio,; : commota vehementi metu mens,. —
Absol.: commorat omnes nos,: cum aliqua species utilitatis objecta est, commoveri necesse est,one must be affected by it, it must make an impression on one,: nihil me clamor iste commovet,: si quos adversum proelium et fuga Gallorum commoveret,: in commovendis judiciis,; cf.: commotus ab oratore judex,: qui me commorit, flebit,provoke, rouse,: Neptunus graviter commotus,: domo ejus omnia abstulit quae paulo magis animum cujuspiam aut oculos possent commovere,; : dormiunt; pol ego istos commovebo,awake, arouse,: porticus haec ipsa et palaestra Graecarum disputationum memoriam quodammodo commovent,stir up, awaken, revive,.—Of things: aes alienum,to demand,: commotā principis domo,init.: si umquam vitae cupiditas in me fuisset, ego... omnium parricidarum tela commossem?provoked,. —
With in and abl.: qui cum ingeniis conflictatur ejus modi, Neque commovetur animus in eā re tamen,: vidi enim vos in hoc nomine, cum testis diceret, commoveri,: in hac virgine commotus sum,i. e. in love,.—
With ex and abl.: nam cum esset ex aere alieno commota civitas,; Auct. B. Afr. 57, 72.—(ε) With ad and acc.: nec sane satis commoveor animo ad ea. quae vis canenda,: homines ad turpe compendium,.—(ζ) With ut and subj.: adeone me ignavom putas, ut neque me consuetudo neque amor Commoveat neque commoneat, ut servem fidem?: tua nos voluntas commovit, ut conscriberemus, etc.,.—
Of the passions, etc., to rouse, stir up, excite, produce, generate: belli magnos commovit funditus aestus, moved the waves of strife from their foundations, ; cf.: commovere tumultum aut bellum,: misericordiam, invidiam, iracundiam,; cf.: commovere miserationem,; : magnum et acerbum dolorem,: invidiam aliquam in me,: summum odium in eum,: bilem,: multorum scribendi studia,: adfectus,; 5, 8, 3; cf.: adfectus vehementer commotos (opp. lenes),.—

commūnĭco (conm-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. (

To divide something with one, whether in giving or receiving.
In giving, to divide a thing with one, to communicate, impart, to share; esp. freq. of imparting in discourse (very freq. in all periods); constr. usu. aliquid cum aliquo; also inter aliquos, alicui, aliquem aliquā re. cum aliquo de aliquā re and absol.
With aliquid cum aliquo: ut si quam praestantiam virtutis, ingenii, fortunae consecuti sunt, impertiant ea suis communicentque cum proximis,; ; : auxilium

sibi te putat adjunxisse, qui cum altero rem communicat, : suam causam cum Chrysogono,: cum iis praemium communicat, hortaturque ut, etc.,: civitatem nostram vobiscum,: causam civium cum servis fugitivis,: at sua Tydides mecum communicat acta (i. e. me socium sumit actorum),: consilia cum finitimis civitatibus,to make common cause, to take common counsel, commune, consult,: cum plebeiis magistratibus,; ; : curam doloris cum aliquo,.—Of discourse: homo, quocum omnia, quae me curā aliquā adficiunt, una communicem,: ea quae didicerant, cum civibus suis communicare non poterant,; ; ; ; so cum aliquo de aliquā re: Pompeius, qui mecum... de te communicare solet,: is mecum de tuā mansione communicat,: cum compluribus de ratione belli,. —

Aliquid inter aliquos: cum de societate inter se multa communicarent,: socii putandi sunt, quos inter res communicata est,: ut quibus de rebus vellemus, tu tuis, ego meis, inter nos communicaremus,; : communicato inter se consilio, (cf. α); .—
Alicui aliquid, or de aliquā re (in Cic. only when the other party sharing is expressed by cum and abl.; cf. Krebs, Antibarb. p. 250): quibus communicare de maximis rebus Pompeius consuerat, (Dinter, ex conj., quibuscum): hisque omnium domus patent victusque communicatur,; so with redditur,: sibi communicatum cum alio, non ademptum imperium esse, Weissenb. ad loc.: id aut ereptum illis est, aut certe nobis cum illis communicatum,; cf. Halm ad loc.; ; ; ; Ascon.—*
Aliquem aliquā re: communicabo semper te mensā meā,.—(ε) Absol.: nonne prius communicatum oportuit? * ; : et secundas res splendidiores facit amicitia et adversas partiens communicansque leviores,; : ut ad se veniat rationesque belli gerendi communicet,: consilia communicant,; cf. ; ; ; .—
Transf. of things: aliquid cum aliquā re, to join to an equal part, to unite: viri, quantas pecunias ab uxoribus dotis nomine acceperunt, tantas ex suis bonis cum dotibus communicant,: privabo potius illum debito testimonio, quam id cum meā laude communicem,; .—
In late Lat.: cum aliquo or alicui, to have intercourse with an inferior: ne cum peregrinis communicarent,: malis,with evil-disposed persons,: ne communices homini indocto,.—Also alicui rei, to take part in, .—
In receiving, to share something with one, to lake or receive a part, to partake, participate in (also class.).
Aliquid cum aliquo: ut me juves Conmunicesque hanc mecum meam provinciam,; cf.: provinciam cum Antonio,: inimicitias mecum,: qui sibi cum illo rationem communicatam putat,believes that he has all things in common with him,; cf. ; ; cf. . § 5 Zumpt; : haud dubitavit (Thalestris) fateri ad communicandos cum rege liberos se venisse, Vogel ad loc.—
Absol.: primo labores et discrimina, mox et gloriam communicabat,.—
Alicui (late Lat.): altari Christi,to receive the sacrament,; id. contra Cresc. 3, 36.—
In Tertull., acc. to communis, II., to make common, i. e. low, base, to contaminate, defile, ; .

commŏdo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.

Trop.: commoda loquelam tuam,: ita praeceptorem eloquentiae ... se commodaturum singulis,: si te commodaveris mihi,: (arithmetica) avaritiae commodat digitos,fits, adapts,: (servi) nulli sceleri manus commodabunt,: operam suam Prisco ad turpissimum ministerium commodasse,: orationi oculos, vocem, manum,.—Absol.: caecus claudo pede commodat,.—

com-mūnis (comoinis, S. C. de Bacch.), e, adj.
con and root mu-, to bind; Sanscr. mav-; cf.: immunis, munus, moenia
,
that is common to several or to all, common, general, universal, public (opp. proprius, that belongs to one: quod commune cum alio est, desinet esse proprium,; cf. ; ; ; 10, 1, 16; 12, 10, 42; 12, 3, 7; v. also the foll.; freq. in all periods and every species of composition); constr. with cum, dat., inter se, or absol.
Prop.: vetus verbum hoc quidem est: Communia esse amicorum inter se omnia,: vinea vulpibus et hominibus,: sepulcrum Asiae Europaeque Troja,: is fit ei cum Roscio communis,; cf.: alterum nobis cum dis, alterum cum beluis commune est,; .—Esp. freq. in the formula aliquid cum aliquo commune habere: vetustas habet aliquid commune cum multis, amor non habet,: cum rerum naturā... quid habere potest commune... gallinaceum fel,: controversia. quae communes minime cum aliis quaestiones habet,: illum... nihil vobiscum commune habentem,: sciat, se nihil mecum habere commune,: omnia cum amico communia habebit, qui multa cum homine,; ; : nec habet (pecudum natura) quidquam commune cum caelo, Lact. de Ira Dei, 7, 4; 8, 3; ; ; , B: vitium commune omnium est,; cf. ; ; ; : communis imperii (i. e. Romani) fines,; cf. libertas,: salus,: utilitas,: mors,natural,: verba,i. e. prose,: jus gentium, et saep.: vitae ignarus, ignorant of life, i. e. of the customs of society, ; cf.: sensu caret,of a sense of propriety, Heind.; cf.: sit in beneficio sensus communis,; ; ; ; cf. also: communium litterarum et politioris humanitatis expers,: communis locus, euphem.,the lower world,; and for a brothel, Bip.—In plur.: loca,public places,; ; but loci, in philos. lang.,a commonplace, common topic,; ; ; ; ; 5, 12, 15; v. locus.—

In gen., plur.: ut communibus pro communibus utatur, privatis ut suis,: paucis ostendi gemis et communia laudas,publicity,; .—In sing.: de communi aliquid consequi,; so : jus communi dividundo,; cf. Gai ; Dig. 2, 1, 11, § 2 al.—
Esp. = τὸ κοινόν, a community, state: commune Latium, Cinc. ap. Müll.: Commune Milyadum,: Siciliae,, § 114; 2, 2, 59, § 145; 2, 2, 63, § 154: gentis Pelasgae,; cf.: communis Graecia,; and: res communis = respublica, Sisenn. ap. .—
In commune.
For common use, for all, for a common object, end, advantage, etc.: metuere,: consulere,; : conferre,; : vocare honores,i. e. to bestow equally upon patricians and plebeians,: profutura,: laborare (apes),.—Rarely in communi: ponere libertatem,.—
In general, generally (in post-Aug. prose): de jure omni disputandum,; ; ; ; —
Halves! ; .—

That represents the common sentiment, democratic: qui in bello... suo et certorum hominum consilio uteretur, eum magis communem censemus in victoriā futurum fuisse, etc.,.—
Of manners, accessible, familiar, courteous, condescending, affable (kindr. in sense with comis; hence in MSS. very freq. interchanged with it; v. comis): simplicem et communem et consentientem eligi (amicum) par est,; so : communis infimis, par principibus,; so ; cf. communitas.—Comp., dub. (al. comior).—Sup., dub. (al. comissimus).—

In rhet.: commune exordium, quod nihilo minus in hanc quam in contrariam partem causae potest convenire,equally appropriate to either side of a cause,; cf. ; ; .—
In gram.: verbum, a common verb, i. e. one that has both an active and passive signification, ; P.: syllaba = anceps, i. e. either long or short, Don. p. 1389 P.; ib.; ib.: genus,of both masculine and feminine gender, ib. et saep.— Hence, Advv.

Absol.: ut cito commentatus est,i. e. has made up a story,: cum in hortos D. Bruti auguris commentandi causā convenissemus,deliberation,: magi, qui congregantur in fano commentandi causā,.—
With acc.: te ipsum, qui multos annos nihil aliud commentaris, docebo quid sit humaniter vivere,: commentari aliquid et discere,: futuras mecum commentabar miserias, id. poët. Tusc. 3, 14, 29.—
With interrog. clause: ut commentemur inter nos, quā ratione nobis traducendum sit hoc tempus,.—
With de: multos mensis de populi Romani libertate,.—
In partic.
Of the orator's preparation for a speech (freq. and class.).
Absol.: ad quem paratus venerat, cum in villā Metelli compluris dies commentatus esset,: itaque videas barbato rostro eum commentari, Varr. ap. : crebro digitorum labrorumque motu commentari,.—
With acc.: ut quae secum commentatus esset, ea sine scripto redderet eisdem verbis quibus cogitasset,: quae mihi iste visus est ex aliā oratione declamare, quam in alium reum commentaretur,.—
Of writings, to prepare, produce as the result of study, write (rare): quorum alter commentatus est mimos,: eo ipso anno cum commentaremur haec,: Cato de militari disciplinā commentans, id. praef. § 30.— With acc., to discuss, write upon: neque commentari quae audierat fas erat,; cf.: carmina legendo commentando, que etiam ceteris nota facere,.—
Transf.

To imitate, adopt the language of another: Achilem Aristarchi mihi commentari lubet,.—
To meditate, purpose: si cogitaras id, quod illa tropaea plena dedecoris et risūs te commentatum esse declarant,.

Lit.
To remove from a place, to carry away, displace, to start, set in motion, move: neque miser me commovere possum prae formidine,; : facilius est currentem incitare quam commovere languentem,: columnas,: castra ex eo loco,to move forward, decamp,, § 96; cf. aciem,to set the line in motion,; : se ex eo loco,: se domo,: me Thessalonicā,: te istinc,: agmen loco. to force back, cause to retreat, Sisenn. ap. ; so, hostem,; : cervum,: molem,: nummum,i. e. to use in business, (1, 1); : ais, si una littera commota sit, fore tota ut labet disciplina. Utrum igitur tibi litteram videor an totas paginas commovere?.—Sacra, t. t., to move or carry about the sacred utensils, images, etc., for religious use, Serv.; cf. : ancilia,: tripodes,.—Hence, humorously: mea si commovi sacra, if I put my instruments (artifices, tricks, etc.) in motion, . —Prov.: glaebam commosset in agro decumano Siciliae nemo,would have stirred a clod,.—
To set in motion in a place, to move hither and thither, to shake, agitate, disturb.
Of things: magni commorunt aequora venti,: alas,; cf.: penna commota volucris,; . —
Of persons, with se: quis sese commovere potest, cujus ille (sc. Roscius) vitia non videat?can stir,: num infitiari potes te... meā diligentiā circumclusum commovere te contra rem publicam non potuisse,; ; ; cf.: Lanuvii hastam se commovisse,.—
Trop.
(Acc. to I. A.) To move, drive back, distodge, refute, confute: nunc comminus agamus experiamurque, si possimus cornua commovere disputationis tuae,: si convellere adoriamur ea, quae commoveri non possunt,.—
(Acc. to I. B.) To throw into disorder, physical or mental; to unbalance, unsettle, shake, disturb (rare but class.): adflantur alii sidere, alii commoventur statis temporibus alvo, nervis, capite, mente,: perleviter commotus fuerat ... (postea) eum vidi plane integrum,: Bacchi sacris commota, Poët. ap. : commotus habebitur, i. e. mente captus,frantic, crazed,; cf.: commota mens,; ; and: commotus mente,.—
To move in mind or feeling, to make an impression upon, to excite, rouse, shake, disquiet, disturb, affect, etc.
With abl.: commorat hominem lacrimis, Turp. ap. : aliquem nimiā longinquitate locorum ac desiderio suorum,: aut libidine aliquā aut metu,; (12, 26): ludis,: quis enim, cum sibi fingit aliquid et cogitatione depingit, non simul ac se ipse commovit atque ad se revocavit, sentit, etc.,aroused,: et amore fraterno et existimatione vulgi,: adfectibus,: doctā voce,: cujus atrocitate,: vix sum apud me, ita animus commotu'st metu, Spe, gaudio,; : commota vehementi metu mens,. —
Absol.: commorat omnes nos,: cum aliqua species utilitatis objecta est, commoveri necesse est,one must be affected by it, it must make an impression on one,: nihil me clamor iste commovet,: si quos adversum proelium et fuga Gallorum commoveret,: in commovendis judiciis,; cf.: commotus ab oratore judex,: qui me commorit, flebit,provoke, rouse,: Neptunus graviter commotus,: domo ejus omnia abstulit quae paulo magis animum cujuspiam aut oculos possent commovere,; : dormiunt; pol ego istos commovebo,awake, arouse,: porticus haec ipsa et palaestra Graecarum disputationum memoriam quodammodo commovent,stir up, awaken, revive,.—Of things: aes alienum,to demand,: commotā principis domo,init.: si umquam vitae cupiditas in me fuisset, ego... omnium parricidarum tela commossem?provoked,. —
With in and abl.: qui cum ingeniis conflictatur ejus modi, Neque commovetur animus in eā re tamen,: vidi enim vos in hoc nomine, cum testis diceret, commoveri,: in hac virgine commotus sum,i. e. in love,.—
With ex and abl.: nam cum esset ex aere alieno commota civitas,; Auct. B. Afr. 57, 72.—(ε) With ad and acc.: nec sane satis commoveor animo ad ea. quae vis canenda,: homines ad turpe compendium,.—(ζ) With ut and subj.: adeone me ignavom putas, ut neque me consuetudo neque amor Commoveat neque commoneat, ut servem fidem?: tua nos voluntas commovit, ut conscriberemus, etc.,.—
Of the passions, etc., to rouse, stir up, excite, produce, generate: belli magnos commovit funditus aestus, moved the waves of strife from their foundations, ; cf.: commovere tumultum aut bellum,: misericordiam, invidiam, iracundiam,; cf.: commovere miserationem,; : magnum et acerbum dolorem,: invidiam aliquam in me,: summum odium in eum,: bilem,: multorum scribendi studia,: adfectus,; 5, 8, 3; cf.: adfectus vehementer commotos (opp. lenes),.—
In discourse: nova quaedam,to start new doctrines, adduce novelties,.— Hence, commōtus, a, um, P. a., moved, excited, aroused: genus (dicendi) in agendo,; cf.: Fimbria paulo fervidior atque commotior,: incidere in rem commotam (i. e. amorem),: animus commotior,: commotius ad omnia turbanda consilium, Weissenb. ad loc.: Drusus animo commotior,more violent, passionate,; cf.: commotus ingenio,; and: Agrippina paulo commotior,: commoto similis,to one provoked, enraged,; cf. .—Sup. and adv. apparently not in use.

la:other:Commodus.html:
com-mŏdus, a, um, adj.,
that has a due or proper measure; hence,
Object., complete, perfect, of full weight or measure, fit, suitable, due, proper, etc. (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose; most freq. in Plaut.): statura,a tall stature,: capillus,: viginti argenti minae,full twenty, (cf. : minae bonae); : talentum argenti,; Lucil. ap. : novem cyathis commodis miscentur pocula,: alimenta,: capitis valetudo commodior,more firm,; ; and transf. to the person: vivere filium atque etiam commodiorem esse,to be better,.—
Subject., suitable, fit, convenient, opportune, commodious, easy, appropriate for some one or something, favorable, friendly to (in every period and species of composition); constr. with dat. or absol., rarely with ad (v. the foll.).
Of things.
With dat.
Of the purpose or use: curationi omnia commodiora,: nec pecori opportuna seges nec commoda Baccho,.—
Of the person: hoc et vobis et meae commodum famae arbitror,: quod erit mihi bonum et commodum,: nulla lex satis commoda omnibus est (corresp. with prodesse),: primordia eloquentiae mortalibus,: hanc sibi commodissimam belli rationem judicavit,: quae sit stella homini commoda, quaeque mala,—
Absol.: hiberna,: longius ceterum commodius iter,; cf.: commodissimus in Britanniam transjectus,: commodius anni tempus,; cf. : faciliore ac commodiore judicio,: litterae satis commodae de Britannicis rebus,: mores,: commodissimum esse statuit, omnes naves subduci, etc.,.—
With or without dat. pers. in the phrase commodum est, it pleases, is agreeable, = libet: proinde ut commodum est,; : dum erit commodum, : si id non commodum est,; ; Ascon.; 2, 2, 16, § 39; 2, 1, 26, § 65; 2, 3, 70, § 165; ; ; : id si tibi erit commodum, cures velim,; ; .—
With ad and acc. of purpose (very rare): nec satis ad cursus commoda vestis Erat,.—
With sup. in u (rare): hoc exornationis genus ... commodum est auditu,.—
Of persons, serving a neighbor or (more freq.) accommodating one's self to his wishes, useful, serviceable, pleasant, agreeable, obliging, neighborly, friendly, polite, affable, gentle, etc.: mihi commodus uni,; cf. : quemquamne existimas Catone commodiorem, communiorem, moderatiorem fuisse ad omnem rationem humanitatis?: commodior mitiorque,: Apronius, qui aliis inhumanus ac barbarus, isti uni commodus ac disertus,: convivae,; cf.: commodus comissator,; and: commodus meis sodalibus,: homines,: mulier commoda, Faceta,; cf. .—In a double sense with I. supra: ubi tu commoda's, capillum commodum esse credito,.—Poet., of the measure of iambic verse: spondeos in jura paterna recepit Commodus et patiens,sharing the paternal rights with them, in a fraternal manner,.—Hence,
Subst.: commŏdum, i, n.
A convenient opportunity, favorable condition, convenience (rare, but in good prose): nostrum exspectare,: cum tamdiu sedens meum commodum exspectet,; 12, 38, 1: velim aliquando, cum erit tuum commodum, Lentulum puerum visas,when it shall be convenient for you,.—More freq.,
In the connection commodo meo, tuo, etc., per commodum, ex commodo, at, or according to my, thy, etc., convenience, conveniently, at one's leisure: etiamsi spatium ad dicendum nostro commodo vacuosque dies habuissemus,according to our convenience,: quod commodo tuo fiat,; ; : suo commodo me convenire, Caes. ap. : ubi consul copias per commodum exponere posset,: tamquam lecturus ex commodo,; ; so opp. festinanter,.—
Advantage, profit (very freq. in all periods and species of composition): commodum est, quod plus usus habet quam molestiae: bonum sincerum debet esse et ab omni parte innoxium,: ut malis gaudeant atque ex incommodis Alterius sua ut comparent commoda,: ut ex illius commodo meum compararem commodum,; cf. ; : cui tam subito tot congruerint commoda,: (honestatem) ipsam suo splendore ad se animos ducere, nullo prorsus commodo extrinsecus posito, Fragm. ap. Aug. contr. Ac. 3, 7, 15 (IV. 2, p. 470 Orell.): sequi matris commodum,: pacis,: contra valetudinis commodum laborare,to the injury of health,: mea,: in publica peccem,; cf.: populi commoda,.—
Specif., a reward, pay, stipend, salary, wages for public service: veteranorum, Brut. et Cass. ap. : omnibus provincialibus ornamentis commodisque depositis,emoluments,; ; cf.: emeritae militiae,; ; cf. also ; : militibus commoda dare,: tribunatus,: missionum,.—
A favor, privilege, immunity, ; .—
A useful thing, a good: commoda vitae,; ; cf.: cetera opinione bona sunt... proprietas in illis boni non est. Itaque commoda vocentur,: inter commoda illas (divitias) numeratis: atqui eādem ratione ne commodum quidem erunt,. —
Sometimes commodo or per commodum, adverb. antith. to that which is

injurious, without injury or detriment: ut regem reducas, quod commodo rei publicae facere possis,: si per commodum reipublicae posset, Romam venisset,.—

Concr., = commodatum, that which is lent, a loan: qui forum et basilicas commodis hospitum, non furtis nocentium ornarent,; cf. .—
Advv.:
commŏdum, adv. temp. (only in colloquial lang. and post-class. prose writers).
At a fit time, just in time, at the very nick, at the very moment, opportunely, seasonably ( = opportune, εὐκαίρως): ecce autem commodum aperitur foris,: commodum adveni domum,: orditur loqui,: ipse exit Lesbonicus,: εὐκαίρως ad me venit, cum haberem Dolabellam, Torquatus... commodum egeram diligentissime, ; . —
To designate a point of time that corresponds with another, or that just precedes it, just, just then, just now.
Absol.: ad te hercle ibam commodum,; : Taurus, sectatoribus commodum dimissis, sedebat, etc.,: si istac ibis, commodum obviam venies patri,just meet,. —
With postquam or (more freq.) with cum in a parallel clause: postquam me misisti ad portum cum luci simul, Commodum radiosus ecce sol superabat ex mari,: quom huc respicio ad virginem, Illa sese interea commodum huc advorterat,: commodum discesseras heri, cum Trebatius venit,: emerseram commodum ex Antiati in Appiam, cum in me incurrit Curio, B. and K. (al. commode); so with the pluperf. and a foll. cum, ; 13, 30, 2; 10, 16, 1; : adducitur a Veneriis Lollius commodum cum Apronius e palaestrā redisset, B. and K. (Zumpt, commode): cum jam filiae nostrae dies natalis appeteret, commodum aderant, quae muneri miseratis,. —
commŏdŏ, adv. temp., = commodum, a., just in time, seasonably, just at this time (ante-class. and very rare): commodo eccum exit, Titin. ap. P. (i. e. in tempore, Charis.): commodo de parte superiore descendebat, Sisenn. ib.: commodo dictitemus, Plaut. Fragm. ap. ; cf. p. 177.—
commŏdē, adv.
(Acc. to commodus, I.) Duly, properly, completely, rightly, well, skilfully, neatly, etc. (class.): suo quique loco viden' capillus satis compositu'st commode?: commode amictus non sum, id. Fragm. ap. : saltare, Nep. praef. § 1: legere,; cf. in comp., : multa breviter et commode dicta,; cf. ; ; ; : cogitare,: audire,: valere,: feceris commode mihique gratum, si, etc.,: commode facere, quod, etc.,; in comp.: commodius fecissent tribuni plebis, si, etc.,.—In medic.: commode facere,to do well, be beneficial,.—
(Acc. to commodus, II.)
Conveniently, suitably, opportunely, fitly, aptly, appropriately: magis commode quam strenue navigavi,: ille satis scite et commode tempus ad te cepit adeundi,: vos istic commodissime sperem esse,: explorat, quo commodissime itinere valles transiri possit,: hoc ego commodius quam tu vivo,; cf.: consumere vitiatum commodius quam integrum,; : cui commodissime subjungitur,; cf. .—
In a friendly manner, pleasantly, gently, kindly: acceptae bene et commode eximus,; ; .—
(Equiv. to commodum, adv. b.) Just, just at the moment when, etc.; only v.l. in the doubtful passages cited supra, commodum, b. fin.
